sources.title: Gudrun Dahl and Anders Hjort-af-Ornäs, Precolonial Beja: A Periphery at the Crossroads (2006)
sources.note: Full scholarly paper read, Nordic Journal of African Studies 15(4), 473 to 498. Medieval territorial names and claimed kingdoms are critically assessed, PDF pages 9 to 11; caravan provisions at Aydhab, PDF pages 12 to 13. Do not adopt the paper’s older automatic Blemmyes/Beja equation or its introductory timelessness rhetoric.

sources.title: Al-Maqrizi, al-Khitat, Part IIa, translated by Karl Stowasser, edited by Bauden and Almon (2022)
sources.note: Primary medieval compilation in annotated translation, chapter 32. Printed pages 289 to 292 treaty of 831 and translators; pages 294 to 296 pastoral movement, al-Masudi’s account dated 943/944 and intermarriage. The compiler preserves earlier accounts. Hostile religious/racial judgments and spectacular troop numbers are not repeated as facts.

sources.title: Cooper, Whiting, Czyżewska-Zalewska and Rammutloa, Pastoralists, travellers and miners at Khor Rafit (2026)
sources.note: Primary excavation report, Azania 61(1), 40 to 80, DOI 10.1080/0067270X.2025.2586366. Repository abstract and indexed primary PDF passages read: unpaginated advance PDF page 8 millstones, page 29 pottery; full PDF direct retrieval failed. Abstract supports 2019 fieldwork and watering station. Claims do not identify each inhabitant ethnically. Indexed witness PDF: https://repository.up.ac.za/server/api/core/bitstreams/156a197d-0700-4e85-859d-a8fc26a6dde2/content .

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Beja te saqwit, object 1996.455
sources.note: Full institutional object record and audio transcript read. Mid-twentieth-century divider, 152.4 by 435.6 cm, cotton/leather/beads/cowrie/doum palm/dye. Female relatives make it for betrothal; daytime and nighttime areas; protective significance. Clearly later evidence, not a medieval object.

sources.title: Mohamed-Tahir Hamid Ahmed, Proverbs Attributed to Humans and Nonhumans in the Beja Language (2024)
sources.note: Full primary linguistic/ethnographic study read at /article/download/1207/639/3696, Nordic Journal of African Studies 33(3), 236 to 256. Abstract: 214 proverbs, 43 nonhuman speakers. Example 21, printed page 250, hyena and donkey story, citing Adarob 1972 page 66; contextual analysis follows. Do not assign these recorded proverbs to a specific medieval century.

sources.title: Klaus Wedekind, Charlotte Wedekind and Abuzeinab Musa, Beja Pedagogical Grammar (2008)
sources.note: Full primary grammar direct PDF read, publication metadata DOI 10.18716/ojs/aaeo/2008_3527, published 22 February 2008. Compiled Aswan 2004/Asmara 2005. Paragraph 20 Atman dialect; paragraphs 23 to 27 phonological Latin transcription, bold vowels mark pitch; PDF page 197 (zero-based 196), Want table immediately before paragraph 386: Hadhiib aharriiw. / I want some bread. Plain-text sample omits typographic bold pitch marking, not segmental letters. No guessed Arabic-script reconstruction.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Shared as broad ethnocultural labels and explicitly phased medieval coverage, not as two proven dynasties or one continuous kingdom. Earlier Blemmyes record remains separate.
batchIdentityNotes.geometry: Bega 700 to 800 bounds 34.526 to 38.756 E, 15.534 to 21.128 N. Beja People 900 to 1000 bounds 31.747 to 39.206 E, 5.527 to 18.561 N: substantial southern overextension through Ethiopia, publicly disclaimed. TopoJSON decoded in identities.json.
batchIdentityNotes.chronology: No dates of founding or extinction inferred. Third period gives later medieval continuity beyond imported window. Household object and linguistic/storytelling examples explicitly dated to modern evidence.
batchIdentityNotes.writing: Exact primary grammar wording and paired English translation, human PDF page 197, Want table. Uses Latin transcription without source typography for pitch; no invented medieval inscription or Arabic glyphs.
batchIdentityNotes.evidenceLimits: The 2006 paper’s discussion of medieval labels warns that outsiders sometimes included speakers of other languages. Khor Rafit is regional archaeological context, not automatically an exclusively ethnic Beja settlement. Primary medieval author hostility and inconsistent troop totals excluded.
